book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook usually defines CRR and SLR together, states their purpose as monetary tools and then gives the legal ranges. Here the video builds one picture from the bank's NDTL: a first arrow to a vault held by RBI (CRR), a second arrow to a safe kept by the bank (SLR), so where the money sits and whether it earns is clear before any law. The purpose of SLR comes as a bank-run what-if. Then it walks the law (ranges, 2007 amendment) twice, once per ratio and once as an era table, then the history curves with the 1991 committee as the cause of each turn, then the wider SLR securities (closing a question it left open at 112 s). The policy use (raise to cool inflation, cut to support growth) comes almost last, after today's numbers are worked into the 77.5% lendable share.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Cut by ratio and by rule change: for each reserve say where the money sits, whether it earns and why it exists, then its legal band and each dated change with the law or committee that caused it; the policy effect comes last from today's numbers.

opening.what: Recalls the last video: NDTL, and that every bank must deposit a share of it with RBI as CRR, in cash; the screen shows the bank's NDTL and an arrow down into a gold vault held by the RBI coin.

moves.what: A second mandatory reserve ratio, SLR, yaani statutory liquidity ratio: a share of NDTL kept safe by the bank itself in gold, cash or government securities.

moves.concept: SLR: share of NDTL kept by the bank in gold, cash or G-secs as a bank-run cushion
moves.what: The part kept for bad times: if many customers suddenly come to withdraw, yaani a bank run, the bank sells these liquid assets to pay them and avoid failing.

moves.concept: SLR: share of NDTL kept by the bank in gold, cash or G-secs as a bank-run cushion

moves.what: Because the 1991 Committee on Financial Systems advised keeping CRR at 3-5%; that is why it kept falling after 1991.

moves.concept: raising or cutting CRR/SLR to control inflation or support growth
moves.what: If RBI raises CRR and SLR, banks have less to lend, so liquidity and inflation can be controlled.

moves.concept: raising or cutting CRR/SLR to control inflation or support growth
moves.what: Inflation is not always bad: the economy needs a little to grow.

moves.concept: raising or cutting CRR/SLR to control inflation or support growth
moves.what: To raise inflation (growth), RBI cuts CRR and SLR, banks lend more, people's purchasing power rises, demand is created, inflation rises (framing 'RBI wants to raise inflation' is odd).

moves.what: Banks report reserves every 15 days; if not maintained RBI penalises, and the penalty is so high that banks borrow for a day or two in the call money market or overnight at repo.

narration.density: About 25 terms and figures (NDTL, CRR, cash, interest on CRR, legal range, amendment 2007, SLR, statutory, gold, G-secs, liquid assets, bank run, income, Committee on Financial System, Narasimham, 3-5%, 38.5%, 25%, 1997, SLR securities, corporate bonds, CDs, commercial paper, state development loans, multilateral securities, NABARD/SIDBI, 77.5%, purchasing power, inflation, reserve ratio, fortnightly report, penalty, call money) in about 690 s, about 3 per minute, many of them numbers and years. The legal part is repeated (per ratio, then as a table), which slows the middle, while the most useful part (policy effect) gets under a minute.

talmel_summary: The opening picture shows the meaning: one NDTL splits into a vault held by RBI (cash, 0% interest) and a safe kept by the bank (gold, cash or G-secs, earns income), and later today's numbers land on those same arrows. Law changes are shown on the number they change (band struck, '<= 15%' written), the 1991 committee points at the turning point on the curve, and a 1999-2007 bar shows the interest window. But from about 200 s the screen is mostly text that copies the speech: an era table built cell by cell, recommendation bullets and a six-line list of SLR securities, often appearing 1-3 s before the words. Only 8 of 24 tiles land together; 13 are picture-first. The policy effect (raise or cut the ratios) has no picture of its own. Tile 19 falls in a 4 s transcript gap and tile 21 just after a 13 s gap.

voice.notes: About 178 words per minute, the calmest of these five, with a reading cadence in the legal part ('1949 se lekar 2007 tak ke is period mein...'). Numbers read as ranges ('3% to 15% of NDTL', '0 se lekar 40%') and decimals ('38.5', '4.5%'). One open-loop line ('iska answer abhi ke liye aap no samjhiye') and one direct question to the viewer before the 77.5% sum. The inflation part is quicker and more conversational ('aur kyunki inflation hamesha kharab nahi hota').

game_ideas.player_does: Splits a bank's NDTL of 2000 crore: drags money into the CRR vault at RBI, into the SLR safe (choosing cash, gold or G-secs), and into the lending pool, under rules set by RBI (for example CRR 4.5%, SLR 18%).
game_ideas.process_happens: An income meter runs: the vault earns 0, the safe earns a little, loans earn most; then a bank-run event sends a queue of depositors to the counter and the safe's liquid assets are sold to pay them.
game_ideas.win: Meet both ratios, survive the bank run and end with the highest income.
game_ideas.lose: Keeping less than the rule triggers the fortnightly report's penalty loop; too little in the safe makes the bank fail the run.
game_ideas.concept: SLR: share of NDTL kept by the bank in gold, cash or G-secs as a bank-run cushion

game_ideas.player_does: Plays RBI with CRR and SLR dials facing a scenario card (prices rising fast, or a slowdown).
game_ideas.process_happens: The lendable share of NDTL recomputes (100 - CRR - SLR), the rain of loan arrows to the borrower crowd thickens or thins, and a demand and inflation meter follows.
game_ideas.win: Bring inflation or growth into the target band with the right direction of change.
game_ideas.lose: Cutting the ratios while prices are already rising pushes the inflation meter into the red, with the chain 'more loans, more purchasing power, more demand'.
game_ideas.concept: raising or cutting CRR/SLR to control inflation or support growth

game_ideas.player_does: Places rule cards (CRR 3-15%, CRR up to 15%, interest on CRR 1999-2007, SLR 25-40%, SLR up to 40%) into the era table and moves the committee figure to the right turning point on the CRR and SLR curves.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each correct card fills its cell; placing the committee at 1991 makes the curves bend down and the SLR circle slide from 38.5% to 25% at 1997.
game_ideas.win: All rules in the right era and the committee at the right turning point.
game_ideas.lose: Putting the floor removal before 2007 shows the law icon refusing ('the amendment came in 2007').
game_ideas.concept: 1991 committee and the fall of SLR from 38.5% to 25% by 1997

checks_learned: Legal sources named in a script must be checked against the book (here both ratios are tagged 'RBI Act 1949'; CRR is usually under the RBI Act 1934 and SLR under the Banking Regulation Act 1949).
Every 'current value' (CRR 4.5%, SLR 18%) must carry its date and be compared with the run date; stale values are flagged.
Eligibility lists (which assets count as SLR securities) must be verified against the source before narration; this list looks wrong.
A recap table should not be rebuilt cell by cell right after the same rules were taught (about 100 s here); reveal it whole as a summary.
Lists of more than about 4 items should become a sort-into-groups scene or icons, not lines of text written one by one.
A policy effect (what changing the ratio does) must get its own scene: the dial moves and the lendable arrow shrinks or grows.
An open-loop question ('for now take the answer as no') must be closed later in the same script; pair them in a check (done here at 415 s).
Framing check: 'RBI wants to raise inflation' should read 'RBI accepts some inflation to support growth'.
Re-transcribe BIE's narration; a gap of more than 10 s without words (508-522 s here) flags a dropped line.

teaching_best.why: One source, two homes: NDTL splits into a vault held by RBI (cash, 0% interest) and a safe kept by the bank (gold, cash, G-secs, earns income), so the CRR-SLR difference is seen before it is stated.
The purpose of SLR comes as a bank-run what-if with the term 'bank run' named right after the scene.
An open question ('for now, no') creates a pull that is paid off later with SLR securities.
History curves are tied to an actor: the committee points at the 1991 peak, and the SLR circle jumps from 38.5% to 25% at 1997, showing advice followed by result.
A direct question with today's numbers (4.5% + 18%) produces 77.5% lendable, drawn as a third arrow raining loans onto borrowers, then turned into the policy cause chain.
Names and corrects a common wrong idea: inflation is not always bad.

teaching_weak.why: Both ratios are tied to an 'RBI Act 1949'; doubtful legal source.
About 100 s rebuilding the same rules as a text table, cell by cell, right after teaching them.
A six-line text list of SLR securities, with doubtful content (corporate bonds, CDs and CPs are generally not SLR-eligible).
Current values given without a date; they have since changed.
The policy use, the most exam-relevant idea, comes near the end, is under a minute, and has no picture of its own.
About 13 s of speech lost in the transcript, right where the list is tied back to the picture.
